text: Make two columns right now for whatever is taking up most of your head. Left: what depends entirely on you (your judgement, your effort, your word, your desire). Right: what does not (the body, reputation, position, what other people decide). Be ruthless sorting them. How much of today's energy went into the right-hand column?
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 1

text: This morning, before getting up, say to yourself: today I will meet a meddler, an ingrate, an arrogant man, a cheat, an envious man, someone who cannot be lived with. Write down who that person concretely is in your day today, and prepare now, in writing, how you will answer them without letting them take your composure.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, II.1

text: Practise the premeditation of evils on something specific you are afraid to lose. Write it as already lost: it has happened, it is done. Describe your life the following day in practical detail. What would you still have? What would you have to learn? Imagining it in advance takes away the part of the blow that is surprise, which is usually the worst part.
source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, 91 and 107 (premeditatio malorum)

text: Go up. Look at yourself from the roof of your house, then from the neighbourhood, then from the country, then from space. From there, today's worry is one dot among millions of dots that are also worrying. Now come slowly back down and write what part of your problem survived the journey and what evaporated on the way.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, VII.48 and IX.30 (the view from above)

text: Before sleeping, be your own judge without being your own executioner: what fault of mine did I cure today? Which vice did I stand against? In what am I better than yesterday? No excuses and no self-flagellation — go through the whole day, and forgive what is already done.
source: Seneca, On Anger, III.36 (the evening review)

text: It is not things that disturb you but your opinions about things. Take whatever irritated you most yesterday, write the bare fact in one sentence with no adjectives, and then write separately everything you added to it. Compare the two texts: which of them is the one that kept you awake?
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 5

text: You could leave life right now: let that determine what you do, what you say and what you think. If today were the last, what on your plan would still stand, and what would fall off the list on its own for being ridiculous?
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, II.11

text: No one loses any life other than the one they are living, nor lives any other than the one they lose. Even if you lived three thousand years you could only lose this instant. Write what someone who had truly understood that sentence would do differently today.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, II.14

text: Remember that you are an actor in a play whose author is not you. This is the part you were given: this body, this family, this period, this health. Write what exactly your current part is, and what it would mean to play it excellently without spending energy complaining about the casting.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 17

text: Never say of anything 'I have lost it', but 'I have given it back'. Think of something or someone no longer in your life and rewrite their story with the verb to return in place of the verb to lose. What changes in your chest when you change the verb?
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 11

text: What stands in the way becomes the way. Take the most irritating obstacle of your week and write which specific virtue it is asking you to practise: patience, courage, justice, temperance? Then write the first action that exercises it.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, V.20

text: Give today over to practised poverty: eat the plainest food, wear the humblest clothes, do without one comfort. At night write this question: is this what I was afraid of? And a second: how much of my anxiety is built on the fear of losing things I have discovered today I do not need so much?
source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, 18

text: It is not that we have little time, but that we waste much of it. Reconstruct yesterday hour by hour and mark with a cross every stretch you did not choose. Add up the crosses. Who did you give those hours to, and in exchange for what?
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life, I

text: Amor fati: do not wish things to be as you want them, want them to be as they are. Write the fact of your current life you resist most, and then write, with all the honesty you can manage, what would open up if you stopped spending your strength denying it.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 8; Nietzsche's formulation

text: Someone spoke badly of you. Epictetus would say: they did not know everything, because had they known they would have mentioned your other faults too. Write down the criticism that stings most, keep whatever grain of truth it holds, and write what you would do with that grain if you were not busy defending yourself.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 33 and 48

text: Think of someone famous two hundred years ago whose name nobody remembers today. Now write: which part of what you do, do you do in order to be remembered? What would you do if you were absolutely certain nobody will remember your name in a hundred years?
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, IV.19 and IV.33

text: Time is a river of events: a thing has hardly appeared before the current has carried it off, and another comes. Write three things in your life that five years ago seemed settled and no longer exist. Which of the things that seem settled today will be on that list five years from now?
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, IV.43

text: Before undertaking anything today, say: I will do this, if nothing prevents it. Write your most important plan of the week, adding that reserve clause to the end of every sentence. What changes in the way you hold the plan when the outcome stops being your property?
source: Stoicism: the reserve clause (hypexairesis); Seneca, On Tranquillity of Mind, XIII

text: Be angry in writing, in full, with whoever wronged you. Now read it back and apply the Stoic filter: did that person mean to harm you, or did they do what seemed right to them out of ignorance? Nobody errs willingly. Write the scene again from that premise.
source: Seneca, On Anger, II; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, II.1

text: Describe yourself as one thing among things: a body that eats, digests and ages, with borrowed opinions and inherited habits. This exercise in physical definition takes the shine off whatever hypnotises us. Apply it today to the object of your strongest desire or your strongest fear: describe it taken apart into its pieces.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, VI.13 (objective definition)

text: Each morning, when getting up is hard, remember: I was not born to keep myself warm under blankets. Write today what exactly you get up for, in one sentence without rhetoric. If you cannot find the sentence, that is today's exercise.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, V.1

text: Draw the circles of Hierocles: you at the centre, then your family, your friends, your neighbours, your fellow citizens, humanity. The work consists of pulling the outer circles inward. Choose someone from a distant circle and write what you would do this week to bring them one circle closer.
source: Hierocles, the circles of oikeiosis (Stoicism)

text: If you are going to the public baths, prepare yourself: there will be shoving, splashing, thieving. Apply it to your day: write the list of predictable annoyances ahead (the traffic, the meeting, the same message as always) and decide your response in advance. Surprise is the door anger comes in through.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 4

text: Choose an object or a person you are strongly attached to. When you kiss your child, Epictetus said, tell yourself quietly: tomorrow they may die. Not to make yourself miserable, but to love without the blindness of believing it is permanent. Write how you would look at that person today with that awareness switched on.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 3

text: Write the list of your current desires. Now sort them: which are natural and necessary, which natural but unnecessary, which neither. The last kind have no bottom. How much of your life is organised around a desire with no bottom?
source: Epictetus and the Hellenistic tradition; cf. Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus

text: Do not talk about how a good man should be: be one. Take a principle you defend out loud and write about the last time you betrayed it in private, with no witnesses. Without punishing yourself: just write what made it easy.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, X.16

text: Take an inventory of what you owe other people: who taught you to read, who fed you without charging, who corrected you in time. Marcus Aurelius opened the Meditations with this exercise, thanking each person for something specific. Write your own Book I: five people, five specific debts.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book I

text: Live each day as a complete day and not a fragment: whoever has finished their day does not fear tomorrow. Write what today is missing before you could say at eleven at night: this day is already whole, even if there is no other.
source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, 12 and 101

text: Imagine a god grants you exactly what you most want today, but hands you in the same lot everything that comes with it: the obligations, other people's envy, the fear of losing it. Write the full invoice. Would you still sign?
source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius, 119; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, VI.51

text: Withdraw inward: there is no retreat quieter or less troubled than one's own soul. Write today what your inner refuge is like: which sentences furnish it, which principles hold it up. If you go to step inside and find nothing there, write what you would have to build this week.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, IV.3

text: Seneca wrote that we have two homelands: the one we were born into and the world. Write what concrete obligation the second imposes on you today that the first does not, and whether you are meeting it.
source: Seneca, On Leisure, IV; Stoic cosmopolitanism

text: Write the letter you would send a friend going through exactly what you are going through. Do not spare them the hard advice. Now read it as though it had been sent to you. Seneca wrote his letters to cure himself while curing Lucilius.
source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius (the letter as therapy)

text: Today, do not try to make things go your way. Just watch what happens inside you when they do not. At night, write the exact anatomy of one small frustration: what you thought first, what you felt, how long it lasted, what dissolved it.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion, 8; the practice of attention (prosoche)

text: Put yourself in the place of whoever offended you and write their version of events in the first person, with their reasons, which seem good to them. Not to absolve them: to understand that their mistake is not a personal attack on your worth.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, VII.26

text: Everything you can see will change and cease to exist. Think it through with your house, your city, your trade, your face. Now write what you do with that truth: does it paralyse you, free you, give you urgency? The Stoics used that awareness to act better today, not to stop acting.
source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, VIII.5 and XII.21

text: Sartre said we are condemned to be free, and that bad faith consists of pretending we are not choosing. Write a situation where you tell yourself 'I have no choice'. Now list the choices you do have and the real price of each. Having no choice is almost always the refusal to pay a price: name it.
source: Jean-Paul Sartre, Being and Nothingness (bad faith)

text: Nietzsche proposes the heaviest weight: a demon tells you that you will live this same life, with every pain and every joy, innumerable times. Would you throw yourself down and curse, or say 'never have I heard anything more divine'? Write which exact part of your current life you could not bear to repeat, and what you will do with that information.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science, 341 (eternal recurrence)

text: Camus says we must imagine Sisyphus happy: lucid awareness of the absurd leads not to suicide but to revolt. Write what your rock is, the one you push each day knowing it will roll back. Then write what there is in the pushing that belongs to you alone.
source: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus

text: Simone Weil wrote that absolutely pure attention is prayer, and that it consists of emptying yourself to let the other in as they are. Choose a person you believe you know well. Write what you would learn about them if you suspended everything you already think you know. What would you ask them from that emptiness?
source: Simone Weil, Waiting for God and Gravity and Grace (attention)

text: Kierkegaard: life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards. Write about an episode of your past you only understand now. Then write what you are living now without understanding it, and trust that it too will have its retroactive meaning. Can you act without waiting to understand?
source: Søren Kierkegaard, Journals (1843)

text: Montaigne asked 'what do I know?' and made doubt a method. Take the firmest conviction you hold about yourself. Write three experiences from your own life that contradict it. Not to destroy it: to make it honest.
source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, 'Que sais-je?'

text: Heidegger distinguishes living according to the impersonal 'they' (one does this, one thinks that) from living as one's own. Write three important decisions of your life and ask of each: did I make it, or did the 'they'? Who exactly is that 'they' in your case — your parents, your profession, your class?
source: Martin Heidegger, Being and Time (das Man and authentic existence)

text: In Buddhism, the first arrow is unavoidable pain; the second one you fire at yourself with your reaction to the pain. Write this week's first arrow in a single sentence. Then write every second arrow you added: the rumination, the reproach, the comparison, the forecast.
source: Sallatha Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 36.6), the simile of the two arrows

text: Aristotle says we are what we repeatedly do, and that virtue is a habit. Do not ask what you want to be: write what you are being, according to the record of your last seven days. Then choose a single small repeatable act that starts manufacturing the person you want to be.
source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, II

text: Levinas says the face of the other addresses me before I decide anything: their vulnerability commands me not to kill them. Write about a person you have turned into a function (the waiter, the one who answers the phone, the one in your way). What would happen if you saw their face?
source: Emmanuel Levinas, Totality and Infinity (the ethics of the face)

text: Nietzsche calls ressentiment the morality of those who, unable to act, turn their impotence into moral superiority. Write bravely about where there is ressentiment in you: what do you despise today that deep down you want and cannot get?
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality, first essay

text: Husserl proposed the epoché: bracketing what we take for granted and describing experience as it gives itself. Choose an everyday object in your house and describe it for ten minutes as if seeing it for the first time, without naming it by its function. What happens to your attention while you do it?
source: Edmund Husserl, Ideas I (phenomenological reduction)

text: Merleau-Ponty says I do not have a body, I am my body, and that the body knows things consciousness does not. Write what your body is saying today: where it tightens, what it avoids, what posture it takes with certain people. Which of your opinions does your body know before you do?
source: Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Phenomenology of Perception

text: Everything compounded falls apart: anicca. Write a list of five things in your life you cling to as though they were permanent. Beside each, write what would change in the way you enjoy it if you fully accepted that it is on loan.
source: Buddhism, impermanence (anicca); Mahaparinibbana Sutta

text: Kierkegaard describes despair as not wanting to be oneself, or desperately wanting to be a self one is not. Write which of the two applies to you more today, and how it shows in your ordinary life — in concrete gestures, not abstractions.
source: Søren Kierkegaard, The Sickness Unto Death

text: Montaigne wrote that to philosophise is to learn to die, and also that death worries us more from a distance than up close. Write a letter to your own death: tell it what you ask of it, what you fear, what you are grateful for, and what you would want to have finished before it arrives.
source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, I.20

text: Buber distinguishes two ways of saying the world: I-Thou and I-It. With It I use, classify, exploit; with Thou I enter into whole relation. Write how many of yesterday's interactions were I-It. Pick one and describe what it would take to turn it into I-Thou tomorrow.
source: Martin Buber, I and Thou

text: Ortega wrote: I am myself and my circumstance, and if I do not save it I do not save myself. Write what your circumstance is today, without complaining about it, and what saving it would mean exactly, as opposed to fleeing from it.
source: José Ortega y Gasset, Meditations on Quixote

text: Spinoza says that each thing strives to persevere in its being, and that freedom is understanding the causes of our affects. Take an emotion that ruled you this week and write its full genealogy: what caused it, what fed it, what would have defused it. To understand is already to change.
source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, parts III and IV (conatus and the bondage of the affects)

text: Hannah Arendt calls natality the human capacity to begin something new, to interrupt the chain of causes. Write which chain in your life (family, work, mental) is running on sheer inertia, and what act would interrupt it.
source: Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition

text: Simone Weil distinguishes affliction (malheur) from mere suffering: affliction marks the soul, isolates, and makes the one who suffers it invisible to others. Write about someone invisible around you. What would it take for their affliction to reach you without them having to shout it?
source: Simone Weil, The Love of God and Affliction

text: Nietzsche quotes Pindar: become what you are. It is not an invitation to comfortable authenticity but to the discipline of giving a character its shape. Write what you would have to stop doing — not what you would have to start — in order to look more like yourself.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Ecce Homo; Pindar, Pythian II

text: Aristotle distinguishes three kinds of friendship: of utility, of pleasure and of virtue. Only the third lasts, because it loves the other for what they are. Classify your five most frequent relationships honestly. How many friendships of the third kind do you have, and what have you done for them lately?
source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, VIII

text: Buddhism calls anatta the absence of a fixed self: you are a process, not a thing. Write the three sentences you use most to define yourself ("I'm the kind of person who..."). Now write one piece of evidence from your life showing that each is only a habit and not an essence.
source: Buddhism, anatta (non-self); Anattalakkhana Sutta

text: Wittgenstein wrote that the limits of my language are the limits of my world. Write about an experience of yours for which you have no word. Invent one and define it precisely, as in a dictionary. What becomes visible when something of yours can finally be named?
source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, 5.6

text: Ricoeur argues that personal identity is narrative: we are the story we are able to tell about ourselves. Write your life in five chapters with their titles. Then ask yourself which stories were left out of the table of contents, and why those in particular.
source: Paul Ricoeur, Oneself as Another (narrative identity)

text: Thich Nhat Hanh speaks of interbeing: in this sheet of paper are the cloud, the forest, the logger, the wheat the logger ate. Take an object you are using right now and write backwards the whole chain of people and elements that made it possible. How does that change your sense of being alone?
source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (interbeing)

text: Sartre: hell is other people — not because they are wicked, but because we see ourselves through their gaze. Write whose gaze you are wearing when you judge yourself. Did you grant them that authority consciously, or did they take it without permission?
source: Jean-Paul Sartre, No Exit

text: Kierkegaard describes the aesthetic stage (living for the interesting), the ethical (living for commitment) and the religious (living for the absolute). Write which one you are living in now, without idealising yourself, and what you would have to risk to make the next leap.
source: Søren Kierkegaard, Either/Or and Stages on Life's Way

text: Aristotelian phronesis is practical wisdom: knowing what to do in this concrete situation, not in general. Recall a recent decision you got right. Write what you perceived in the situation that someone else would have missed. That is your practical wisdom: name it so you can use it again.
source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, VI (phronesis)

text: Pierre Hadot argues that ancient philosophy was not a theory but a set of spiritual exercises meant to transform the way one sees. Write which exercise — not which idea — has actually changed the way you live. And which one you have abandoned without noticing.
source: Pierre Hadot, Philosophy as a Way of Life

text: Montaigne wrote of his friend La Boétie: if I am pressed to say why I loved him, I can only answer "because it was he, because it was I". Write about a bond of yours that you cannot justify with reasons. What does it tell you that there are loyalties without an argument?
source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, I.28, "Of Friendship"

text: Weil said that gravity drags the soul downward as it does bodies, and that only grace rises. Write what your automatic movements of gravity are: complaint, comparison, the quick consolation. What have you seen enter your life that did not come from your own effort?
source: Simone Weil, Gravity and Grace

text: In virtue ethics the question is not "what should I do?" but "what kind of person do I want to become?". Think of someone you truly admire, not for their achievements but for their character. Write the three qualities you admire and one situation this week where you could rehearse one of them.
source: The virtue ethics tradition (Aristotle; Alasdair MacIntyre, After Virtue)

text: Camus distinguishes philosophical suicide (leaping into an explanation that soothes) from living without appeal. Write what certainty you have manufactured so as not to have to bear an open question. Can you hold the question one more day without covering it up?
source: Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus

text: Stoics and Buddhists agree: wanting things to be other than they are is the engine of suffering. But injustice does have to be changed. Write where the border lies today between accepting and resigning yourself, and how you tell one from the other in your own life.
source: The Four Noble Truths (Buddhism) in dialogue with the Stoic dichotomy of control

text: Write what you are reproaching yourself for right now, in your exact words. Then write the same paragraph addressed to your best friend, who has done exactly the same thing. Read both aloud. The distance between the two texts is the exact measure of your self-compassion deficit: what do you gain by keeping it?
source: Kristin Neff, "How would you treat a friend?" exercise

text: Three things that went well today, however small, and beside each one, your part in making it happen. The second half is the important one: this is not an inventory of luck, it is an inventory of agency.
source: Martin Seligman, "Three Good Things" exercise

text: Mental subtraction: pick something good in your life right now and write out in detail the chain of accidents that had to happen for it to exist. Now write your life if just one of those accidents had failed. Gratitude comes more easily through the door of absence than through the door of abundance.
source: Koo, Algoe, Wilson and Gilbert, mental subtraction; Greater Good in Action exercise

text: Write about a part of you that embarrasses you: the one that procrastinates, the one that gets angry, the one that eats at night. Now ask it in writing: what are you afraid would happen if you stopped doing your job? Let it answer in its own words, without correcting it. No part is bad; they all have a positive intention.
source: Richard Schwartz, Internal Family Systems

text: Write a list of everything you are avoiding feeling this week and, beside each item, the concrete manoeuvre you use to avoid feeling it: the phone, the fridge, the series, the extra work, the conversation you are not having. Be literal. Experiential avoidance is not weakness, it is a strategy; write down what it is costing you.
source: ACT, experiential avoidance (Hayes, Wilson)

text: The Japanese ikigai is not an overlap of four circles but something more domestic: the small joys that make getting up worthwhile. Write five tiny things from your week that gave you that push: the seven o'clock coffee, a message, the smell of something. There is no career on this list.
source: Mieko Kamiya, On the Meaning of Life (ikigai ni tsuite)

text: Write your best possible self: a year from now everything has gone reasonably well, you have worked hard and things have settled. Describe that ordinary day in sensory detail for twenty minutes, with no constraint of realism but no magical fantasy either.
source: Laura King, Best Possible Self exercise

text: Think of the last time you felt rejected. Before analysing anything, write a sentence of acknowledgement: this is a moment of suffering. Then: rejection is part of human experience, and right now thousands of people feel this. And finally: what do I need to hear right now, and who can say it, myself included?
source: Kristin Neff, the three components of self-compassion

text: Identify the schema most active in you these days: abandonment, mistrust, emotional deprivation, defectiveness, failure, dependence, self-sacrifice, unrelenting standards, approval-seeking. Write which one it is and then the childhood scene that installed it. Don't analyse it: just tell it as a scene from a film.
source: Jeffrey Young, schema therapy: early maladaptive schemas

text: When you are distressed, do you move toward, move away, or freeze? Write exactly what you do in the first two hours after a conflict with someone who matters. Then write what you did at ten years old when you felt the same. The overlap is usually embarrassing and highly informative.
source: John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth, attachment strategies; Sue Johnson, EFT

text: Write about something that makes you envious. Envy is a dirty but reliable compass: it points at a desire you do not allow yourself to have. What does that person have that you want and do not authorise yourself to want? Who taught you it was not for you?
source: The psychology of values and envy; cf. the psychodynamic tradition and ACT

text: Shame is "I am bad"; guilt is "I did something bad". Take an episode you are still dragging around and write it twice: once in the key of shame and once in the key of guilt. Notice what concrete action becomes possible from the second text, and what paralysis the first one produces.
source: Brené Brown and June Tangney, the shame-guilt distinction

text: Write to yourself in the third person about the problem on your mind: "Anna is going through...", "Michael is finding it hard to...". Linguistic distancing reduces rumination and improves reasoning. Write for ten minutes this way and notice what advice appears that did not appear in the first person.
source: Ethan Kross, distanced self-talk

text: Make a list of your current roles: son, mother, boss, friend, patient, neighbour. Score from 1 to 10 how much energy each one consumes and how much meaning it gives back. Write which role has the worst balance and what you have been avoiding saying about it.
source: ACT, values domains; and role clarification in the psychology of meaning

text: Write the list of your "shoulds" for this week, all of them, unfiltered. Then, in front of each one, write who is saying it: you, your mother, your boss, a version of you from fifteen years ago, a magazine? Cross out the ones you don't recognise as yours and rewrite the ones you do as "I choose".
source: CBT (the tyranny of the shoulds, Ellis) and values work in ACT

text: Frankl said we cannot choose what happens to us but we can choose our attitude, and that life questions us and we answer. Write what your life is asking you this week, phrased as a direct question, and what a worthy answer would be.
source: Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning; logotherapy

text: Write a letter to your body. Not about it: to it. Thank it for something concrete it does for you without being asked, apologise for something, and ask it what it needs this week. Then write its reply.
source: Expressive writing applied to body image; the somatic tradition

text: Identify the loudest protector in your internal system: the critic, the perfectionist, the controller, the one who dissociates. Write its CV: when it started work, in which crisis it became indispensable, what disaster it has spent years preventing. End by thanking it for the shift and asking whether it would accept reduced hours.
source: Richard Schwartz, IFS: protector parts (managers and firefighters)

text: Write about someone you have not forgiven. Don't force yourself to forgive: first write, in detail, exactly what they owe you. Put it in the form of an invoice. Then write what it costs you every month to go on being the creditor of that debt.
source: Everett Worthington, the REACH model of forgiveness

text: Which of your needs have you left unnamed for so long that you no longer even feel it? Write it as a concrete request to a concrete person, in the exact words you would use. You don't have to send it. Just check whether you can put it into words.
source: Marshall Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication: needs and requests

text: Write what you do when nobody is watching and nobody is going to assess you: a whole free Sunday, no obligations and no witnesses. That is usually where what you truly value lives, underneath what you think you value. Does it match what you say about yourself?
source: Values clarification in ACT; the psychology of intrinsic motivation (Deci and Ryan)

text: Think of the person you clash with most. Write what legitimate need of theirs lies underneath the behaviour that annoys you. Then write what need of yours, equally legitimate, lies underneath your reaction. Almost no conflict is about needs: almost all of them are about strategies.
source: Marshall Rosenberg, NVC; and Sue Johnson, the negative cycle in EFT

text: Write what you would tell yourself if you knew you had only one year of full health left. Not a year of life: a year of energy. The constraint changes the arithmetic of what you are postponing. What falls off the list, and what moves to first place?
source: The psychology of meaning; cf. Irvin Yalom, Existential Psychotherapy

text: Take the thought that repeats most in your head this week. Write it down. Then write: how long have I had it? Does it move me toward what matters to me or away from it? What would I do today if that thought were present but not in charge? The question is not whether it is true, but whether it is useful.
source: ACT, workability and cognitive defusion

text: Write a scene in which you felt deeply seen by someone. Describe it in sensory detail: where you were, what they said, what loosened in your body. That memory is material: you can return to it when the threat system fires.
source: Paul Gilbert, the soothing and affiliative system in CFT

text: Write an inventory of what you carry for others: tasks, care, silences, money, encouragement. Now write what others carry for you. If the scales are uneven, write what you think would happen if you started asking. Self-sacrifice usually has a belief underneath it: name it.
source: Jeffrey Young, the self-sacrifice schema in schema therapy

text: Think of something you left unfinished that still takes up mental space. Write why you left it, without the official explanation you give other people. Then decide and write one of three sentences: I pick it up again on (date), I bury it today deliberately, or I put it on hold until (date).
source: The Zeigarnik effect; goal psychology (Gollwitzer, implementation intentions)

text: Write about your relationship with rest. What do you think would happen if you really stopped? Who would you be letting down? What idea about your own worth depends on producing? Be specific: name the person who taught you that equation.
source: Schema therapy (unrelenting standards) and the psychology of burnout

text: Write a dialogue between the part of you that wants the change and the part that sabotages it. Give them equal speaking time and forbid yourself from letting the first one win. End the dialogue with a question the saboteur asks the other, one the other cannot answer.
source: IFS (polarised parts) and Gestalt therapy chair work

text: Write about a failure of yours from the angle of what it taught you, with one strict rule: no stock phrases about overcoming adversity. If you cannot find a real, concrete lesson, write that — that there isn't one, and that sometimes things simply go badly.
source: Expressive writing and benefit finding, with the critique of forced positivity

text: Note the three things you are proudest of and ask after each one: who was I trying to prove it to? The answer may be "nobody", and then you have found a clean value. Or it may be a name, and then you have found a debt.
source: The psychology of autonomous motivation (Deci and Ryan) and values work

text: Write which version of you appears when you are with each of three different people in your life. Describe them as if they were three named characters. Which one do you like most? Which one exhausts you? With whom are you the version closest to the one you would want to be always?
source: The psychology of the relational self; IFS and ego state theory

text: Ikigai in four honest questions: what do I love doing, what do I do reasonably well, what does the world around me need, and what would I be paid for? Write a short answer to each and then point out where the real conflict between them lies, because there always is one.
source: The popular ikigai framework (the four-circle diagram), with Mieko Kamiya's caveat

text: Write the list of emotions that were allowed in the home you grew up in and the list of those that were not. Then look at which of the forbidden ones is hardest for you to feel or express today. Write a recent scene in which that emotion showed up and what you did with it.
source: Diane Fosha (AEDP) and experiential therapy: affect phobia

text: Write what you are grateful for today toward someone you have a complicated relationship with. Not to reconcile and not to justify anything: only to check whether you can hold two truths at once about the same person.
source: Gratitude (Emmons) combined with tolerance of ambivalence (dialectical thinking, DBT)

text: At the end of the day, write a single sentence beginning "today was the day when...". Nothing more. Repeat it every night for a month and then read the thirty sentences in a row: you will see the plot of your life that no long entry would have shown you.
source: Minimal expressive writing; the practice of a daily narrative log

text: Pick an object in your line of sight and describe it for ten minutes without ever naming it. You may not say what it is for. Only shape, weight, light, temperature, sound. The point is not a riddle: it is to find out how much you stop seeing the moment you know a thing's name.
source: Francis Ponge, The Nature of Things

text: Sit somewhere public and exhaust what happens: the buses going past, the clothes, who is looking at a phone, what repeats. Don't look for meaning, take inventory. Perec called this exhausting a place, and found that the interesting things arrive once the striking ones have run out.
source: Georges Perec, An Attempt at Exhausting a Place in Paris

text: Write the same minimal scene — someone boards a bus and sits down — three times: in the past tense, as a medical report, and as gossip told by a neighbour. Queneau wrote ninety-nine versions. Three are enough to see that style does not decorate a story: it changes it.
source: Raymond Queneau, Exercises in Style

text: Write a whole paragraph without using the most frequent letter in your language (the e, in English and in Spanish alike). The constraint is not a silly game: by closing off the comfortable words it forces you to find the ones you would never have gone looking for.
source: OuLiPo; Georges Perec, A Void (a novel without the letter e)

text: Write the last sentence first. Only that one, the one you want left ringing. Then write the text that deserves it. Working backwards from the ending removes the worst part of writing, which is deciding where to start.
source: A classic craft practice; cf. Poe, The Philosophy of Composition

text: Tell something that happened to you today in the voice of someone who was there and is not you: the waiter, the dog, the person behind you in the queue. Keep the facts, change only who is looking. What that narrator cannot know is exactly what you were taking for granted.
source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (point of view)

text: Write for ten minutes without lifting your hand or correcting anything, not one comma. If you go blank, write "nothing is coming" until something comes. The only rule is not to stop: editing and inventing use the same part of the brain and get in each other's way.
source: Peter Elbow, freewriting; Natalie Goldberg, Writing Down the Bones

text: Think of something you are afraid to write. Don't write it yet: write why it frightens you, who would read it and what would happen then. The fear almost always has one specific reader with a name. Once you name them, the piece becomes possible.
source: Anne Lamott, Bird by Bird

text: Describe a stranger you saw today in five sentences, and make the fifth contradict the other four. A character starts to exist at exactly the point where they stop being consistent.
source: John Gardner, The Art of Fiction

text: Write a scene in which two people talk about one thing while arguing about another that is never named. All the subtext lives in what they choose not to say. If it reads too clearly, cut one more line.
source: Hemingway's iceberg theory; cf. Chekhov, indirect dialogue

text: Take a memory of yours and tell it as if it were false: invent an impossible detail and keep a straight face to the end. Seeing how much your memory can take without breaking tells you which part of it was already literature.
source: The autofiction tradition; cf. Borges, Ficciones

text: Write a list of twenty things you know how to do that almost nobody around you does: a knot, a dialect, telling an engine by its sound. Don't explain them yet. That list is your exclusive material, and it usually sits unused.
source: Lynda Barry, Syllabus; the inventory as a quarry

text: Write a full page in sentences of fewer than eight words. Not one subordinate clause. When you finish, read it aloud: the short rhythm is not poor, it is a different way of breathing, and some of your long sentences were only a fear of landing.
source: Verlyn Klinkenborg, Several Short Sentences About Writing

text: Describe a place you know well using only the other four senses: no sight. The smell of the entrance hall, how the floor sounds, the air on your face. Sight takes up nearly all writing, which is why nearly all writing looks alike.
source: A classic sensory exercise; cf. Ray Bradbury, Zen in the Art of Writing

text: Write the scene you are ashamed to write, but in the third person and under another name. When you finish, change the names back and see which sentences you can no longer stand behind. Those are the ones to work on, not to delete.
source: Ethan Kross, self-distancing, applied to the writing craft

text: Open a book you love at any page and copy a whole paragraph by hand. By hand, not on the keyboard. Copying is the oldest way to learn rhythm: you will feel where the author breathes and where you would have put a full stop.
source: The practice of copying by hand; Hunter S. Thompson among others, with a medieval precedent

text: Write a whole story in which nothing exceptional happens and the reader still wants to reach the end. Just someone waiting for something that does not arrive. If it works, you have learned that tension is not made by the event but by the expectation.
source: Chekhov; and the tradition of the eventless short story

text: Write three different opening sentences for the same piece: one that starts with a fact, one with a voice speaking, one with a place. Choose afterwards, not before. We usually lose the best opening by writing the first that comes to mind.
source: Workshop practice; cf. Italo Calvino, Six Memos for the Next Millennium

text: Describe someone you love without a single evaluative adjective: no kind, generous, difficult. Only what they do, what they say and what they keep quiet. The portrait will come out more exact, and probably more uncomfortable.
source: Show, don't tell; cf. Flannery O'Connor, Mystery and Manners

text: Write a letter you will not send, as raw as you like, then write the version you would actually send. Keep both. The distance between them is your public voice, and it is worth knowing exactly how much it lies.
source: Expressive writing applied to style; cf. Lincoln's unsent letters

text: Take a word you heard today and write its whole invented history: who said it first, in what situation, how it got deformed. A false etymology, carefully made. There is no better exercise for breaking the habit of treating words as if they were transparent.
source: The tradition of fantastical etymology; cf. Borges and Cortázar

text: Write about a moment when you changed your mind about something important, but tell it as a scene, not as reasoning: where you were, who said what, what you did with your hands. Ideas are remembered when they have a body.
source: Scene versus summary; cf. Vivian Gornick, The Situation and the Story

text: Make an arbitrary rule for today's piece and obey it to the end: every paragraph starts with the same word, or there is no first-person verb, or everything happens within one square metre. An arbitrary constraint yields more discoveries than total freedom, which mostly yields the usual.
source: Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt, Oblique Strategies; the OuLiPo method

text: Write the worst first draft you can: clumsy, sentimental, overblown, every cliché in it. On purpose. Lamott called it the shitty first draft and said it is compulsory. Writing badly on purpose is the only reliable way to start.
source: Anne Lamott, Bird by Bird ("shitty first drafts")

text: Write a scene in the present tense and then the same scene in the past. Read them one after the other. The present presses and allows no perspective; the past orders and cools. Choosing a tense is not grammar: it is deciding how far away you put the reader.
source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (tense and distance)

text: Take something you wrote months ago and remove one word in every three without changing any of the others. Read what is left. It nearly always improves, and that stings just enough to teach you something.
source: The practice of cutting; cf. Stephen King's "kill your darlings"

text: Write about what you don't remember: the gap of an afternoon, a face rubbed out, the name that won't come back. Don't fill it in with invention. Describe the exact shape of the hole. Honestly written memory has more holes than facts.
source: The memoir-essay tradition; cf. Perec, W, or the Memory of Childhood

text: Write a full page of dialogue with no attributions: no "said", no gestures. Only what they say. If on rereading you cannot tell who is speaking, the problem is not the attributions: it is that both voices are yours.
source: A classic dialogue exercise; cf. Elmore Leonard, Ten Rules of Writing

text: Describe someone's work by watching them do it: the baker's hands, the mechanic's, the person cutting your hair. Only the movement, no admiration. Other people's competence described precisely is one of the hardest things to write and one of the most welcome to read.
source: Cf. Richard Sennett, The Craftsman; and the tradition of trade reportage

text: Write a piece beginning "I have never told anyone that..." and don't stop for five minutes. Then decide calmly what to do with it: publish it, keep it, delete it. Writing it and deciding about it are two separate acts, and confusing them is what leaves us mute.
source: James Pennebaker, expressive writing

text: Turn something that angers you into a numbered list, dry, without adjectives. Only the facts, one per line. Anger arranged as an inventory stops being a vent and starts being an argument — and sometimes starts being funny.
source: The list as a literary form; cf. Umberto Eco, The Infinity of Lists

text: Write a scene in which the weather does exactly the opposite of what the character feels: a funeral on a glorious day, good news under hail. Having the weather match the mood is so worn out it has become invisible; the contrast is not.
source: Against the pathetic fallacy; cf. John Ruskin, who named it

text: Tell a story that was told to you and is not yours: a grandparent's, a colleague's, a stranger's on a train. Write it with respect for the facts and freedom with the rhythm. Being the keeper of other people's stories is a craft too.
source: Studs Terkel, oral history; Svetlana Alexievich

text: Write for fifteen minutes starting from the sentence already in your head right now, even if it is nonsense or a shopping list. Don't judge it. The blank page is not beaten with inspiration, it is beaten by getting in wherever you can.
source: Julia Cameron, The Artist's Way (morning pages)

text: Write what you would write if you knew nobody would ever read it, and then what you would write if you knew everybody would. Compare the two lists. In the gap between them sits exactly the book you have not written yet.
source: Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet; the question of whether you would write the same with no readers

text: Draw the house of your childhood in your head and walk it room by room. Pick one room and describe all of it: the floor, the light in mid-afternoon, where the socket was, what could be heard from there. Start with the floor plan; memories come hanging off the architecture.
source: Georges Perec, Species of Spaces; the method of loci

text: Write about something you inherited: who had it before, how it reached you, where it is now. And then the uncomfortable question: do you keep it because you like it, or because you don't dare let it go?
source: Material culture and family memory; cf. Edmund de Waal, The Hare with Amber Eyes

text: What is your first memory? Write it in all the detail you can and then mark honestly which parts are memory and which are photographs or things you were told. Almost no first memory is first-hand, and that does not make it any less yours.
source: The psychology of autobiographical memory; childhood amnesia

text: Write about the first time you said no to someone with power over you: a parent, a teacher, a boss. What happened afterwards, and what you learned that day about the price of saying it.
source: Autobiographical turning points; the developmental psychology of autonomy

text: Pick one specific year of your life and write what it smelled of: the food in that house, the detergent, the car, the street. Smell is the only sense wired straight into the limbic system, which is why it brings back the whole memory instead of the summary.
source: The Proust effect; olfactory memory

text: Write about someone who mattered to you for a short time and whom you never saw again. What they gave you, what you took, why it ended. Not every relationship that shaped you lasted.
source: Brief bonds in the narrative of the self; cf. Ricoeur, narrative identity

text: Which dish takes you straight back to a place? Write out the recipe as if explaining it to someone and let the memory slip in between the steps. Family recipes are historical documents disguised as instructions.
source: Culinary memory; cf. the family recipe-book tradition

text: Write about the day you stopped believing something you had been taught at home. Not the conclusion: the day, the scene, who was in front of you. Changes of belief have a date even when we tell them as processes.
source: Rupture moments in autobiographical memory

text: Describe one of your grandparents doing something ordinary: not a portrait, a three-minute action. How they sat, how they peeled a piece of fruit, what their hands did while they talked. If you can't remember, write that too.
source: Portrait through action; intergenerational memory

text: Write about a place you cannot return to: because it no longer exists, because it changed hands, or because you are no longer the person who used to walk in. Describe it as it was, in the present tense, until it runs out.
source: Topophilia and loss; cf. Gaston Bachelard, The Poetics of Space

text: Which song takes you back to an exact period? Write where you heard it, who with, and what was happening in your life then. The involuntary soundtrack of a life says more than a list of favourite songs.
source: Autobiographical musical memory; the reminiscence bump

text: Write a list of every house you have lived in, with how long you spent in each. Then pick the one that took the least time and that you remember most, and ask yourself why that one.
source: Autobiographical cartography; the inventory of addresses

text: Write about one specific summer of your adolescence. Only one, and only that summer: who was there, what you did in the afternoons, what you were waiting to happen. Adolescence is remembered better than any other age, and it is worth using that.
source: The reminiscence bump: we remember ages 15 to 25 disproportionately

text: Write about a job you had and would not take again. The colleagues, the smell of the place, what you learned without meaning to. Bad jobs usually leave better material than good ones.
source: Work memory; cf. Studs Terkel, Working

text: Write about a scene you witnessed rather than starred in, and that stuck with you without your quite knowing why. Don't interpret it: tell it. What memory keeps without asking permission usually has its reasons.
source: Involuntary memory; cf. Proust, In Search of Lost Time

text: What frightened you as a child? Write it from the inside, with the logic it had then, without explaining it from your current age. Childhood fears are coherent; what fails is the information, not the reasoning.
source: Memory of childhood fear; developmental psychology

text: Write about a lie you told years ago that was never found out. What you were protecting with it. And whether you would say the same today or would no longer need to.
source: Moral memory; the self that judges itself over time

text: Describe the handwriting of someone in your family. How they made capitals, whether they pressed hard, whether the line slanted. And what they wrote: lists, notes, birthday cards. Handwriting is the closest thing to a voice that the dead leave behind.
source: Everyday written culture and grief

text: Write about the first time you saw the sea, or a mountain, or a big city. Not what you felt: what you saw, in order, as you were arriving.
source: Perceptual first times; travel writing

text: List the things that were done in your house that you thought were normal until you found out nobody else did them. Customs, invented words, odd schedules. A good part of what shaped you is in there.
source: Domestic anthropology; the family idiolect

text: Write about a goodbye you did not know was the last one: the last time you played in the street, saw someone, stood in a place. Last times almost never announce themselves.
source: Cf. the notion of the "last time" in autobiographical memory

text: Write what you wanted to be when you grew up at eight years old, and what exactly attracted you about it. Not the profession: the specific detail you liked. That detail is often still alive somewhere you did not expect.
source: Continuity of early motivations; vocational psychology

text: Write about a day that was ordinary and that you remember in full. No drama, no event. And ask yourself what fixed it: it is nearly always a combination of light, company and the absence of hurry.
source: Episodic memory of the everyday

text: Write a letter to the person you were exactly ten years ago. Don't give them advice: tell them what happened. The advice is for you; what they are owed is the news.
source: Letters to the past self; writing the self across time

text: Write about money in your house when you were small: whether it was talked about, how, who decided. No figures needed. What you learn about money as a child is more like a grammar than an account.
source: Early economic socialisation

text: Describe the walk to school, step by step, with the corners in order. You will find that body memory outlasts names: your legs remember streets whose names you have forgotten.
source: Spatial and procedural memory

text: Write about a teacher who marked you, for better or worse, and be specific: what exactly they said, in which class, in front of whom. A thirty-second sentence can last forty years.
source: School memory; the disproportionate weight of adult remarks

text: Write about a friendship that cooled without a fight. The hard part with these is that there is no break-up scene to tell, only a list of times you didn't call. Write it anyway.
source: The dissolution of bonds without conflict

text: What were you wearing on an important day of your life? Start with the clothes and pull the thread: who chose them, where you put them on, what became of them. Clothes date memories better than the calendar does.
source: The material memory of clothing

text: Write about something that mortified you at fifteen and looks minor today. Not to laugh at that person: to notice that shame has a shelf life, and that today's will have one too.
source: Temporal perspective on shame

text: Write the story of how your parents met, or whoever raised you, exactly as you were told it. Then mark which parts are clearly a tale polished by time. Every family has its founding mythology.
source: Family myths and oral transmission

text: Write about a decision you made quickly that changed years of your life. Reconstruct the minute before: what you knew, what you didn't, why you didn't think about it longer. Big forks rarely look big from the inside.
source: Biographical turning points

text: Write about a tradition you no longer keep: a meal, a date, a ritual. Tell how it was and when it stopped. Traditions are not abandoned by decision, they are abandoned by an accumulation of years when it just didn't happen.
source: Domestic ritual and its disappearance

text: Pick a photograph of yourself you know well and write what the photograph does not show: the minute before, who took it, what happened afterwards. A photograph fixes an instant and erases the rest; a diary does the opposite.
source: Cf. Roland Barthes, Camera Lucida

text: Write what you want someone to remember about you in fifty years, and then what they are actually going to remember. They tend to be different lists, and the second is the more interesting one.
source: Posthumous memory; cf. the distinction between the remembering self and the experiencing self (Kahneman)

text: Look at the sky for three minutes, properly, then describe it without using the word blue or the word cloud. You will have to notice edges, depth, how it changes from one side to the other. Almost nobody has looked at the sky today.
source: An attention practice; cf. John Ruskin, who taught cloud drawing in order to teach seeing

text: Watch an animal — a bird, a dog, an insect — for five minutes and write what it does without attributing a single human intention. It is harder than it sounds, and the discipline of not projecting is exactly what lets you see the animal.
source: Ethology; cf. Konrad Lorenz and the critique of anthropomorphism

text: Walk with no destination for twenty minutes, turning whenever you feel like it, then write the five things you would not have seen if you had been going somewhere. Having a destination is a very efficient way of seeing nothing on the way.
source: The situationist dérive; Guy Debord

text: Write about a plant you see every day and whose name you don't know. Describe it precisely, then look it up. Learning the name after looking is a different thing from looking after learning the name.
source: Cf. Robert Macfarlane, Landmarks; and naturalist practice

text: The nearest stone to you is older than any living thing you have ever known. Write what was happening in the world when it formed, even if you have to imagine it, and how it feels to be passing over something that slow.
source: Deep time; cf. John McPhee, who coined the term, and James Hutton

text: Write about the water you drank today: where it came from, what it passed through, how long it has been in circulation. No water molecule is new. You have drunk water that was in a glacier and in the body of someone you never met.
source: The hydrological cycle; cf. popular accounts of the water cycle

text: Listen for two minutes with your eyes closed and list every sound, ordered from nearest to furthest. The furthest one you can identify tells you the real size of the place you are in.
source: Soundscape; R. Murray Schafer, The Soundscape

text: Describe today's light: its colour, its hardness, which way the shadows fall and what time it started to change. Painters have organised their working day around this for centuries, and most of us cannot tell eleven in the morning from six in the evening.
source: The painterly practice of light; cf. the Impressionists and Monet's series

text: Write about one specific tree you know. How old it might be, what it has watched go past, who planted it. And if it is still there when you are gone, who will look at it.
source: Tree longevity; cf. Peter Wohlleben, The Hidden Life of Trees

text: Write what the weather is doing today as if explaining it to someone who lives in another climate and cannot picture it. No meteorological terms: what the air does on your skin, what clothing is too much, what is possible today and what is not.
source: Writing everyday weather; cf. Thoreau's weather journals

text: Think of the last time you really saw the night sky, far from a city. Write what occurred to you there that does not occur to you here. Light pollution does not only hide stars: it hides a way of thinking.
source: Cf. Paul Bogard, The End of Night

text: Pick something small off the ground — a leaf, a stone, a screw — and describe it for ten minutes as if it were the only thing left of our era and you had to explain it to whoever came next.
source: The object as document; the archaeology of the everyday

text: Write about the season we are in right now, but skip the cliché: what is actually happening out there this particular week, what has opened or closed or left. Seasons are not four, they are fifty-two.
source: Phenology, the study of annual cycles; cf. the Japanese calendar of seventy-two micro-seasons

text: Write about the ground you stand on: what is under these tiles, what was here two hundred years ago, what was dug out to put in what you now use. Every city is built in layers and the only one we see is the top.
source: Urban stratigraphy; cf. the archaeology of living cities

text: Describe today's sunrise or sunset if you saw it, and if you didn't, write that: how many days it has been since you saw either, and what you were doing instead.
source: Circadian rhythms and indoor life

text: Write about an animal that lives in your city and that you don't count as wildlife: pigeons, rats, gulls, wild boar. Describe it with the respect you would give a documentary. The wild has not left, it has adapted.
source: Urban ecology; cf. Menno Schilthuizen, Darwin Comes to Town

text: Write what you ate today and where each thing came from: which plant, which animal, which country, how many hands. No moralising. Just the chain, as complete as you know it, and the gap where you don't.
source: Cf. Michael Pollan, The Omnivore's Dilemma

text: Write about today's wind, or its absence. Where it comes from, what it moves, what sound it makes in which materials. Wind is the hardest thing to describe because you only see it in what it touches.
source: Describing the invisible; cf. Lyall Watson, Heaven's Breath

text: Go out at night and write what only exists at night in your neighbourhood: which lights are left, who is working, which animals come out, how the sound changes. The same place has two versions and we only know one well.
source: Night ethnography; cf. the tradition of the nocturnal flâneur

text: Write about something you have watched grow or rot over days: a plant, a forgotten piece of fruit, building work in the street. Describe the change, not the state. Almost everything we write is a photograph of something that is really a film.
source: Longitudinal observation; cf. naturalists' field notebooks

text: Write about the last time you got soaked by rain you hadn't planned for. What you did: ran, took shelter, kept walking. And how old you were the last time rain struck you as good news.
source: The sensory experience of weather; body memory

text: Your body holds more bacterial cells than human ones, and not one of the cells you had ten years ago is exactly the same. Write what that does to the idea that you are a single thing with a clear edge.
source: The microbiome and cell turnover; cf. the holobiont debate

text: Write about an everyday phenomenon you can't explain: why the sky changes colour, why ice floats, why a bulb hums. Write your own hypothesis first and then look it up. Having a hypothesis before you search changes what you understand.
source: Learning through prior prediction; science pedagogy

text: Write about the most complete silence you can remember. Where you were, what could be heard inside the silence (there is always something) and what went through your head. Absolute silence does not exist: what exists is the absence of us.
source: Cf. Gordon Hempton, One Square Inch of Silence

text: Write a description of your street as someone arriving from very far away would write it, having never seen anything like it. Take nothing as known: what those boxes on wheels are, why people walk in a line down one side.
source: Defamiliarisation; Viktor Shklovsky, Art as Device

text: Look at the palm of your hand for a whole minute, as if it were not yours, and describe it. It is the part of you that you have seen most and looked at least.
source: Attention to one's own body; contemplative practice

text: Write about what can be seen from the nearest window, with one rule: only what has changed since yesterday. If you think nothing has, look for five more minutes.
source: A daily observation practice; cf. Thoreau's notebooks

text: Write about a mountain, a river or a coastline you know, and about what it was like ten thousand years ago. That landscape you take for the fixed backdrop of things is really one frame of something moving very slowly.
source: Geomorphology; cf. Marcia Bjornerud, Timefulness

text: Write down which animals, plants or insects are in the room with you right now, counting the ones you can't see. You are never alone in a room; you are only without company at your own scale.
source: Domestic biodiversity; cf. Rob Dunn, Never Home Alone

text: Write about the last time you felt small in front of something: a storm, a cathedral, a clear sky, the sea. Awe shrinks the self for a while, and that is probably its function.
source: The psychology of awe; Dacher Keltner, the "small self"

text: Describe a material with your hands rather than your eyes: the wood of that table, the fabric of that chair, the metal of the handle. Close your eyes, touch it for a minute, then write. Touch has a very poor vocabulary, which is why it needs the exercise.
source: Cf. Juhani Pallasmaa, The Eyes of the Skin

text: Write about something broken or abandoned that you see often: a crooked shutter, an empty lot, a car that never moves. How long it has been like that, what grows on it, who left it. Decay is the one thing that happens without anyone organising it.
source: The aesthetics of ruin; cf. modern ruins and the ecology of abandonment

text: The sunlight that fell on you today left the Sun's core tens of thousands of years ago and its surface eight minutes ago. Write what that makes you feel, if it makes you feel anything, and be honest if the answer is nothing.
source: Solar physics; the photon diffusion time

text: Write about the landscape you see when you close your eyes and think "somewhere I'd like to be". Describe it as if it were real: the temperature, the ground, the noise. Then ask yourself when you were there, or where you got it from.
source: Inner landscapes; affective geography

text: Write today's weather-and-nature report in five lines, as if you were your street's chronicler: temperature, light, what had bloomed or fallen, what animal you saw. Do it daily for a year and you will have something no weather service keeps.
source: The phenological diary; the tradition of amateur naturalist recording

text: Write what you learned today by doing something badly. Not the mistake: what the mistake taught you about how the thing works. Nearly all practical knowledge arrives that way, and almost nobody writes it down.
source: Cf. Richard Sennett, The Craftsman: learning through failure

text: Describe a movement in your work that now comes without thinking and that used to be hard. Break it into steps as if you had to teach it. You will see how difficult it is to explain what you already know: that is tacit knowledge.
source: Michael Polanyi, The Tacit Dimension ("we know more than we can tell")

text: Write what your parents did for a living, or whoever raised you, and which part of their trade stuck to you even though you do something else: the way of measuring, of dealing with a customer, of tidying up at the end. Trades are inherited sideways.
source: Intergenerational transmission of practical knowledge

text: Write what you would do with your work if nobody paid you for it: which part you would keep, which would be the first to go. The answer does not tell you whether to quit; it tells you where the core is.
source: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation; Deci and Ryan

text: Describe the tool you use most, be it a knife, a keyboard or a spreadsheet. What you have changed about it, what habits you have with it, what you would do if it were gone tomorrow. Working tools end up shaped like their owner.
source: Cf. Sennett on the relation between hand and tool

text: Write about someone you learned your trade from. Not what they taught you: how they taught it. Whether they let you fail, corrected you in front of others, explained things or simply worked while you watched.
source: Learning by observation; the apprenticeship tradition

text: Write which part of your work you would be embarrassed to show someone who admires you. No judgement: just name it. It is nearly always the part you have known for years ought to be fixed.
source: Craft standards and professional honesty

text: Write about the last time you did something really well and nobody noticed. Describe it in technical detail, without playing it down. Good work that goes unseen needs at least one witness, and today you can be it.
source: Cf. Matthew Crawford, Shop Class as Soulcraft: good work as its own standard

text: Write the vocabulary of your trade that an outsider would not understand: five words and what they actually mean. Then look at which of them you use in order to avoid having to explain yourself.
source: Professional jargon; the sociolinguistics of work

text: Write how you know when something is finished. Not when it is due: how you yourself know it is done. If you have no criterion of your own, you are borrowing someone's, and that is a good place to start looking.
source: Internal quality criteria; cf. the ethics of the craftsman

text: Describe your working day in blocks of real time, not what you had planned. How much was craft, how much coordination, how much waiting. The gap between what you think you do and what you do is usually the whole problem.
source: Time-use studies; cf. time diaries in the sociology of work

text: Write about a work problem you solved and could not explain how. Reconstruct the hunch: what you had seen before that resembled it. Expert intuition is compressed memory, not magic.
source: Gary Klein, naturalistic decision making; recognition-primed decisions

text: Write what you would tell someone starting out in your field that appears in no manual. The thing that takes years to learn and, with luck, twenty seconds to pass on.
source: Practical know-how and oral transmission in the professions

text: Write about a rule at work that you follow without knowing why it exists. Interrogate it: does it protect against something real, or is it the fossil of a problem that is gone? Both answers are useful.
source: Cf. Chesterton's fence: don't remove a fence until you know why it was put up

text: Write about the physical side of your work, even if you think it has none: where it hurts at the end of the day, which posture you repeat, what your eyes do. Every trade leaves a mark on the body, including the ones done sitting down.
source: Ergonomics and the embodiment of work

text: Write about a colleague from whom you learned something that wasn't technical: patience, how to say no, how to run a meeting. Trades are learned in company, and that part never shows up on a CV.
source: Situated learning at work; Lave and Wenger, communities of practice

text: Write what would disappear if you were not in your post. Not what would stop being done: what would be done differently and worse without anyone knowing why. That is your real contribution, and it rarely matches the job description.
source: Tacit organisational knowledge

text: Write about the worst professional advice you were given and why it sounded good. Bad advice is rarely stupid: it is usually good advice from another era, or another job.
source: The transfer of rules out of context

text: Write which part of your work a machine will do within ten years and which part it won't. Be concrete and be honest in both directions: overstating the danger and denying it are the same way of not thinking about it.
source: Automation and tasks; cf. the occupations-versus-tasks distinction in labour economics

text: Write about a trade that has all but vanished and that you saw practised: a knife grinder, a linotypist, a switchboard operator, a cobbler. Whatever you remember, however little. What is not written down is lost in one generation.
source: The memory of vanished trades; oral history of work

text: Write about a time you got something wrong and said so, and what happened next. If you never have, write why not. The culture of a workplace is measured exactly there, not on its website.
source: Amy Edmondson, psychological safety in teams

text: List the things you do at work because they have always been done that way. Mark which ones you would still do if you started from scratch today. The difference is the dead weight you drag around every week.
source: Process debt; cf. the critique of "we've always done it this way"

text: Write about the difference between being busy and working, with examples from this week. It is not a moral distinction: they produce different kinds of tiredness and only one of them leaves something finished.
source: Cf. the deep-work / shallow-work distinction (Cal Newport)

text: Write about the invisible work that holds yours up: who cleans, who invoices, who answers the phone, who cooked what you ate. Name them if you know their names. If you don't, write that too.
source: Care work and invisible labour; cf. the sociology of reproductive work

text: Write about a skill you had and lost through disuse. How long it took you to notice, and whether you miss it or are only annoyed at having lost it. They are not the same thing.
source: Skill decay; the psychology of expertise

text: Write how you start working: the exact order of the first ten minutes. Coffee, email, window, chair. That ritual is not wasted time, it is what tells your head it has begun; worth knowing what yours is so you don't break it by accident.
source: Starting rituals; cf. Mason Currey, Daily Rituals

text: Write about something you made with your hands that still exists: a piece of furniture, a meal, a repair, a garden. And about how it feels to be able to point at the result. A good deal of modern work's unease fits in that sentence.
source: Cf. Matthew Crawford on agency and the visible result

text: Write the question you always get asked at work and how you now answer it without thinking. Then answer it properly, in writing, as if it were the first time. Automatic answers go stale without warning.
source: The erosion of thought through repetition

text: Write about the last time you were absorbed in what you were doing and lost track of time. Which task it was, how hard it was, what was around you. That state can be engineered if you know what produced it.
source: Mihály Csíkszentmihályi, flow

text: Write who your work serves. Not the company: the specific person at the end of the chain. If you cannot name anyone, write why the chain broke and at which link.
source: Adam Grant, on perceived impact and meaning at work

text: Write about a time a client, a patient, a student or a user taught you something about your own trade. What they said and why it was hard to accept.
source: Learning from the recipient; the critique of expert-user asymmetry

text: Write what you would do on the first Monday if you were given a paid year with no obligation to work. And in the second month. The first answer is the rest you are owed; the second tells you what your real trade is.
source: A classic question in vocational clarification

text: Write the story of how you ended up doing what you do, told honestly: with the accident in it, the grant that came through, the person who called. Almost no career is a plan; almost all of them are told afterwards as if they were.
source: John Krumboltz, planned happenstance theory

text: Write what you would like whoever takes your job to learn from you when you leave. Write it as you would write it to that person. It is the most useful document you can leave behind, and almost nobody writes it until it is too late.
source: Knowledge transfer in organisations

text: Write what doing things well means to you, with a definition you can apply to a specific task tomorrow. No abstract excellence: what you would check, what you would not let through, how much extra time you would give it.
source: Cf. Sennett: the craftsman as one who does things well for the sake of doing them well
